title: Flying on Thanksgiving Day: What to Know Before You Book
summary: Flying on Thanksgiving Day may mean smaller crowds, but timing matters. Compare the benefits, risks and tips before booking your holiday flight.
body_markdown:
Flying on Thanksgiving Day can be a good choice if you want to avoid the largest airport crowds, but it may not fit your needs if your plans depend on a tight arrival time or several connections.


Here is how to decide whether a Thanksgiving Day flight fits your trip.
‍


## **How Busy are Airports on Thanksgiving Day?**


Thanksgiving Day is typically quieter at U.S. airport security checkpoints than the busy travel dates surrounding it.


According to[TSA’s final 2025 checkpoint totals](https://www.tsa.gov/travel/passenger-volumes/2025) , the agency averaged about 2.48 million screenings per day. Thanksgiving Day’s 1.56 million screenings were 37% below that average. By comparison, the Tuesday and Wednesday before Thanksgiving were 8% and 11% above average, while the following Sunday was 26% above average.


For 2026, CLEAR expects Friday, November 20, to be the busiest pre-Thanksgiving travel day, followed by Wednesday, November 25. Sunday, November 29, is expected to be the season’s busiest travel day as travelers return home. Airport security lines are expected to peak from 5 to 7 a.m. and remain busy until about 6 p.m. local time.


That contrast can make Thanksgiving Day appealing, but crowd size is only one part of the decision. Your flight time, route, connections, and plans after landing matter just as much.
‍


## **Benefits of Flying on Thanksgiving Day**


### **You May Avoid the Largest Airport Crowds**


Many travelers leave on Tuesday or Wednesday so they can reach their destination before Thanksgiving morning. By Thursday, much of that outbound rush has passed.


A quieter terminal may mean shorter lines at check-in, bag drop, airport security, and food counters. Conditions still vary by airport and time of day, so do not assume every checkpoint will be empty.


### **You May Find a Better Fare**


On some routes, Thanksgiving Day flights can cost less than the most popular Wednesday departures. Prices depend on the airline, destination, and booking date, so compare the full trip rather than looking only at the outbound flight.


The return can change the total considerably. The Sunday after Thanksgiving is often one of the busiest travel days of the year, so a lower Thanksgiving Day departure fare may be offset by an expensive Sunday return.


### **An Early Flight Can Preserve Much of the Holiday**


A morning nonstop may let you avoid a busy departure day without missing the full celebration. This works best when the airport is close to your destination and someone can pick you up soon after landing.


Work backward from the time you need to arrive. Include the flight, possible delays, baggage claim, and transportation from the airport, not only the scheduled landing time.
‍


## **Drawbacks of Flying on Thanksgiving Day**


### **A Delay Could Disrupt the Celebration**


A flight that arrives two hours late on a normal travel day may be inconvenient. On Thanksgiving, it may mean missing dinner or other plans that cannot move.


Weather, aircraft issues, and delays from earlier flights can affect the schedule even when the airport feels quiet. If arriving on time is essential, traveling a day earlier gives you more flexibility if disruptions arise.


### **You May Have Fewer Backup Flights**


Airlines may operate fewer flights on a holiday than on a typical weekday. If your flight is canceled or you miss a connection, the next available option may leave later than you expect.


A nonstop flight reduces the number of places your trip can go off schedule. If you need a connection, allow a comfortable buffer and review other flights on the route before booking.


If an airline cancels or significantly changes your flight and you choose not to travel or accept an alternative, you may be entitled to an automatic refund under[U.S. Department of Transportation rules](https://www.transportation.gov/individuals/aviation-consumer-protection/refunds) .


### **Some Airport Services May Have Limited Hours**


Restaurants, shops, lounges, rental car counters, and public transportation may follow holiday schedules. Confirm the services you expect to use at both airports, especially if you have an early departure or late arrival.


Bring a snack, refillable water bottle, and portable charger so you do not have to rely on airport businesses being open.


### **The Return Trip Can Be More Difficult**


The easiest outbound day does not always create the easiest round trip. Returning on Sunday may place you in the busiest part of the Thanksgiving travel period.


If your plans are flexible, compare Friday, Saturday, Monday, and Tuesday returns. An extra day away or a shorter visit may help you avoid the largest return crowds.
‍


## **Who Should Consider Flying on Thanksgiving Day?**


A Thanksgiving Day flight may work well if you can take an early nonstop, have flexible gathering plans, and are traveling a short or familiar route. The trip may also be easier when you can travel with a carry-on, have more than one way to reach your destination after landing, and return on a day other than Sunday.


Leaving earlier may be the better choice if you must arrive by a specific time, need multiple connections, or are checking essential items. Consider traveling before Thursday if winter weather could affect your route, backup flights are limited, or a delay would cause you to miss the main reason for the trip.
‍


## **How to Plan a Thanksgiving Day Flight**


### **Choose the Earliest Practical Nonstop**


Early flights are less likely to be affected by delays that build throughout the day. A nonstop also removes the risk of missing a connection.


Do not choose an uncomfortably early flight simply because the fare is lower. Make sure you can reach the airport with enough time for parking, bag drop, and airport security.


### **Check the Full Door-to-Door Schedule**


Look beyond the departure and arrival times. Account for the drive to the airport, baggage claim, rental car pickup or ground transportation, and the trip to your final destination.


For example, if your Thanksgiving dinner starts at 3 p.m., landing at noon may not leave enough time once you include the steps above.


### **Pack Essentials in Your Carry-On**


Keep medications, chargers, travel documents, a change of clothes, and anything you need for the holiday gathering with you. If a checked bag is delayed and you need to leave the airport in order to make it to your Thanksgiving dinner, you will still have the essentials.


Confirm TSA and airline rules before packing food, gifts, liquids, or batteries.


### **Make a Backup Plan Before You Leave**


Know which later flights serve your route and how you would reach your destination if your original plans change. Save your airline’s contact information and turn on flight notifications.


Discuss the backup plan with the people meeting you so everyone knows what to do if your arrival time changes.

## **Should You Book a Flight on Thanksgiving Day?**


Flying on Thanksgiving Day can be a good idea when a quieter airport, possible fare savings, and an early nonstop flight fit your plans. It is a bigger risk when you need to arrive at a fixed time, depend on several connections, or have few backup flight options.


Compare the entire round trip, not only the outbound fare. If you decide to fly on Thursday, choose a schedule with room for delays and plan each step from home to your final destination.
